propositions.text: The Appellant, a Portuguese citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Portugal, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks the RAD to overturn the RPD decision and find him a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD and to find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Alternatively, the Appellant requests a new hearing before a differently constituted RPD panel.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the matter be returned to the RPD for a new hearing under a differently constituted panel.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not submitted new evidence or requested an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: He has not submitted new evidence in support of this appeal. The Appellant is not requesting an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection, without new evidence or oral hearing, requesting overturn or new hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges he fled Portugal in 2012 fearing harm from former employees threatening him over unpaid wages.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that he fled Portugal in 2012 over fear of harm coming to him by former employees who threatened the Appellant because the Appellant failed to pay the workers their wages earned.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he fled Portugal in 2012 due to threats from former employees over unpaid wages.

propositions.text: The Appellant was arrested in Canada in September 2015 for overstaying his visa.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was arrested in Canada by CBSA in September of 2015 for overstaying his visa.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant was arrested in Canada in September 2015 for overstaying his visa.

propositions.text: At arrest, the Appellant told CBSA he had no fear returning to Portugal but preferred Canada for work opportunities.
propositions.quote: He has no fear in returning to Portugal but does not want to go back since things are bad in Portugal and there is no work," and that "He really likes living in Canada and feels that there are more work opportunities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant told CBSA he had no fear returning to Portugal but preferred Canada for work.

propositions.text: In November 2015, the Appellant told the Minister's Delegate he overstayed because he couldn't support family in Portugal due to no jobs.
propositions.quote: the Appellant stayed in Canada (beyond his visa allowance) because he could not afford to support his family in Portugal because there was no job back home.

propositions.text: The Appellant said he feared people he owed money to wanted to kill him and that his brother advised others would 'deal with him'.
propositions.quote: the Appellant told the Minister's Delegate that he feared that people he owed money to wanted to kill him. In this same interview, the Appellant told the Delegate that on XXXX XXXX, 2015, his brother advised the Appellant that "other guys in Portugal had said they would deal with him (the Appellant)."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant told the Minister's Delegate in 2015 he feared people he owed money to and was threatened.

propositions.text: The Appellant said he would return to Portugal if there was work available in another area.
propositions.quote: If there was work, would you go back to another area of Portugal?" the Appellant replied, "Yes, if there was work, I would go back.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant said he would return to Portugal if work was available elsewhere.

propositions.text: The RPD found the claim not credible, the allegations false, and the threats never made.
propositions.quote: the RPD found that the claim was not credible, that the Appellant's allegations were false and that the alleged threats were never made.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's claim not credible, allegations false, and threats never made.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.

propositions.text: The RAD acts pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of IRPA in confirming the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision denying protection and dismisses the appeal, pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to provide a comprehensive memorandum, leaving the RAD to guess his issues, which is improper.
propositions.quote: Unfortunately, the Appellant has failed to put forward a comprehensive and informative memorandum, leaving the RAD in the position of trying to understand what the Appellant's issues are. This is not the job of the RAD.

propositions.text: RAD Rule 3 requires the appellant's record to contain specific documents and detailed submissions in a set order.
propositions.quote: RAD Rule 3 clearly outlines what an Appellant must do in regards to an appeal record: (3) The appellant's record must contain the following documents, on consecutively numbered pages, in the following order: (a) the notice of decision and written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing; (b) all or part of the transcript of the Refugee Protection Division hearing if the appellant wants to rely on the transcript in the appeal, together with a declaration, signed by the transcriber, that includes the transcriber's name and a statement that the transcript is accurate; (c) any documents that the Refugee Protection Division refused to accept as evidence, during or after the hearing, if the appellant wants to rely on the documents in the appeal; (d) a written statement indicating (i) whether the appellant is relying on any evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Act, (ii) whether the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held under subsection 110(6) of the Act, and if they are requesting a hearing, whether they are making an application under rule 66 to change the location of the hearing, and (iii) the language and dialect, if any, to be interpreted, if the Division decides that a hearing is necessary and the appellant needs an interpreter; (e) any documentary evidence that the appellant wants to rely on in the appeal; (f) any law, case law or other legal authority that the appellant wants to rely on in the appeal; and (g) a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the Refugee Protection Division hearing, (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant, (iv) the decision the appellant wants the Division to make, and (v) why the Division should hold a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the Act if the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant failed to provide a proper memorandum as required by RAD Rule 3, leaving the RAD to guess his issues.

propositions.text: The Appellant only supplied a basic IRB/CISR 3005 form, which is deficient as a memorandum.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has supplied only a filled out copy of IRB/CISR 3005 form which gives only very basic and undetailed information on what the Appellant alleges are issues. This memorandum is deficient; however, I will do my best to work with this for the sake of fairness to the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's memorandum deficient but will try to work with it for fairness.

propositions.text: The Appellant's issue is whether the RPD erred by failing to consider plausible explanations for inconsistencies in his behaviour and statements.
propositions.quote: I believe the Appellant's issue is as follows: 1) Did the RPD err by failing to consider plausible explanations for the inconsistencies in the Appellant's behaviour and statements?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the Appellant's issue as whether the RPD erred in not considering plausible explanations for inconsistencies.

propositions.text: The determinative issues are the Appellant's credibility and state protection as canvassed by the panel.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this appeal is the Appellant's credibility. A second and equally determinative issue is state protection, which was canvassed at the hearing by the panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the determinative issues are credibility and state protection.

propositions.text: The standard of review applied is correctness for questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, per Huruglica.
propositions.quote: For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.

paragraphs.summary: The court applies the correctness standard of review per Huruglica for all questions.

propositions.text: Counsel argues the RPD erred by not considering plausible explanations for inconsistencies in the Appellant's behaviour and statements.
propositions.quote: Counsel argues that the RPD erred when it did not consider what counsel argues is a plausible explanation for inconsistencies in the Appellant's behaviour and statements.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel argues the RPD erred by not considering plausible explanations for inconsistencies in the Appellant's statements.

propositions.text: Counsel argues the combined effect of 2012 and 2015 threats triggered a credible fear in the Appellant.
propositions.quote: Counsel argues that it was a "combined effect" of the threats that the Appellant allegedly received in 2012 and the threat communicated over the phone in XXXX 2015 that triggered a credible and subjective fear in the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel argues the combined 2012 and 2015 threats triggered the Appellant's credible fear.

propositions.text: One month after the 2015 threat, the Appellant said he would return to Portugal if work was available, contradicting fear claims.
propositions.quote: one month after the XXXX 2015 phone threat, the Appellant still told the Minister's delegate that if there was work available in Portugal, the Appellant would return.

propositions.text: This statement contradicts the claim of fear for life due to threats not told to CBSA.
propositions.quote: This statement belies any allegation of being fearful for his life due to threats which the Appellant failed to tell CBSA about when he was interviewed by an agent.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified the 2012 threats mainly caused him to come to Canada in March 2012.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified before the RPD that it was mainly because of the threats of 2012 that he came to Canada in March of 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's 2015 statement contradicts fear claims and that 2012 threats mainly caused his flight.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not mention 2012 threats in his Basis of Claim form.
propositions.quote: I also note that the Appellant did not even mention the 2012 threats in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified the omission was due to a fast translator and CBSA officer not wanting him to think.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified that it was an issue with the translator who spoke very quickly and that the CBSA officer spoke quickly and did not want the Appellant to think.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified the CBSA officer was not present when he completed the BOC with his brother's help.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has testified that the CBSA officer was not present when the Appellant, with the help of his brother, completed his BOC.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appellant omitted 2012 threats from his BOC; the Appellant blames fast translation and CBSA officer absence.

propositions.text: Counsel argues omission of 2012 threats is understandable as Appellant's fear was triggered by 2015 communication.
propositions.quote: Counsel argues that the omission of the critical fact of the 2012 threats from the BOC is understandable as "in the appellant's mind, the original threats in 2012 would have diminished over time and that it was his brother's XXXX 2015 communication that the threat still existed that triggered his fear."

propositions.text: Counsel argues it is not unreasonable the Appellant did not mention 2012 events in the 2015 Minister's Delegate interview.
propositions.quote: Counsel argues that it is therefore not unreasonable that the Appellant did not refer to the 2012 events in the Minister's Delegate review interview which took place in 2015.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel argues the omission of 2012 threats is understandable as the 2015 communication triggered fear and omission in 2015 interview is reasonable.

propositions.text: The court rejects counsel's argument that omission of 2012 threats is reasonable.
propositions.quote: I reject counsel's argument.

propositions.text: It is unreasonable that the precipitating event causing flight was not mentioned in the interview or BOC.
propositions.quote: It is not reasonable that the precipitating event which caused the Appellant to flee his home country, leaving his family behind, would not be mentioned in the interview and certainly not reasonable that such a catastrophic event which would send a man fleeing thousands of miles from his family and his home would not even rate a word in the BOC.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects counsel's argument and finds it unreasonable that the precipitating event was omitted from interview and BOC.

propositions.text: The Appellant provided no evidence other than testimony to substantiate his claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has provided no evidence other than his testimony, to substantiate his claim.

propositions.text: Counsel's argument is weak and implausible that the precipitating event would fade from memory.
propositions.quote: Counsel's argument is weak at best, nonsensical at worst. To suggest that the event which precipitated the Appellant's flight from Portugal would simply fade into the memory is ridiculous.

propositions.text: It is implausible that the Appellant would forget the reason for separation from family and homeland over years.
propositions.quote: Every day that the Appellant was in Canada, he was separated from loved-ones and from his homeland. To suggest that any person would forget about the reason he was so separated in a matter of a couple of years, while living away from loved ones, is implausible.

propositions.text: The court does not accept the explanation for omission of critical information from the BOC.
propositions.quote: I do not accept the explanation for the omission of critical information, central to the reason for his refugee claim, being omitted from his BOC.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence beyond testimony, rejects counsel's argument as weak and implausible, and does not accept omission explanation.

propositions.text: Counsel failed to show how the panel's decisions are errors of fact, law, or mixed fact and law.
propositions.quote: Counsel has failed to indicate how or why the panel's decisions are either errors of fact or errors of law or errors of mixed fact and law.

propositions.text: Counsel only argued an unsubstantiated opinion of error without evidence or case law.
propositions.quote: Counsel has simply argued an opinion (counsel's) of why he believes that the panel's decision is an error. That opinion is not substantiated by any evidence of error or by any case law.

propositions.text: Counsel tells the RAD what he believes is an error but does not show how there is an error.
propositions.quote: Counsel tells the RAD what counsel believes is an error but does not show the RAD how there is an error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds counsel failed to show how the panel erred, only offering unsubstantiated opinion without evidence or case law.

propositions.text: The RPD can make credibility conclusions based on omissions, inconsistencies, implausibilities, and other reasons.
propositions.quote: The RPD is allowed to make conclusions on credibility of witnesses, including claimants, based on such issues as omissions, inconsistencies, implausibilities and other reasons.

propositions.text: Without evidence or case law, the RAD defers to the RPD on credibility where no contrary evidence exists and RPD has advantage.
propositions.quote: Without evidence or at least case law to support counsel's arguments, the RAD will defer on issues of credibility where there is no contrary evidence presented and in the case where the RPD has a distinct advantage over the RAD in making the credibility determination.

propositions.text: This case is one where the RAD defers to the RPD on credibility.
propositions.quote: This is such a case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RPD can assess credibility and the RAD defers to RPD without contrary evidence; this case warrants such deference.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified he has no adequate state protection in Portugal and no viable internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that he has no adequate state protection in Portugal, none would be forthcoming in Portugal and that he will not be able to avail himself of a viable internal flight alternative within Portugal.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to provide documentary evidence supporting his claim of inadequate state protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant failed to adduce any documentary evidence to support his allegation of inadequate state protection.

propositions.text: The RAD must rely solely on the Division's National Documentary Package for information on state protection.
propositions.quote: This leaves the RAD in the position of depending solely upon the Division's National Documentary Package (NDP) for information on state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant testified to inadequate state protection but provided no documentary evidence; the RAD relies on the National Documentary Package.

propositions.text: The 2017 OSAC Crime and Safety Report states Portugal has a relatively low rate of violent crime and professional authorities.
propositions.quote: I note that the 2017 OSAC Crime and Safety Report (U.S. D.O.S.),4 March 2017, states the following: Overall Crime and Safety Report "Portugal has a relatively low rate of violent crime..." Police Response "The authorities are professional..."

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the 2017 OSAC report states Portugal has low violent crime and professional authorities.

propositions.text: The Ministries of Internal Administration and Justice oversee internal security and police forces in Portugal.
propositions.quote: The Ministries of Internal Administration and Justice are primarily responsible for internal security. The Ministry of Internal Administration oversees the SEF, the PSP, and the GNR.

propositions.text: The IGAI investigates security force killings and evaluates justifiability, with civilian oversight and mechanisms to punish abuse.
propositions.quote: The IGAI, responsible to the Ministry of Internal Administration, investigates security force killings and evaluates whether they occurred in the line of duty or were otherwise justifiable. Civilian authorities maintained effective control over the SEF, the PSP, and the GNR, and the government has effective mechanisms to investigate and punish abuse and corruption.

propositions.text: An independent ombudsman and IGAI investigate police abuse complaints; NGOs criticize slow investigations and lack of independent oversight.
propositions.quote: An independent ombudsman chosen by parliament and the IGAI investigates complaints of abuse or mistreatment by police. Nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) criticized the slow pace of investigations and the lack of an independent oversight agency to monitor the IGAI and the Ministry of Internal Administration.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Portugal's internal security structure, oversight mechanisms, and NGO criticisms of investigation pace and oversight.

propositions.text: Portugal is a constitutional semi-presidential democracy with free and fair elections and civilian control over security forces.
propositions.quote: Portugal, which includes the archipelagos of the Azores and Madeira, is a constitutional semi-presidential representative democracy with a president, prime minister, and parliament elected in multiparty elections. National legislative elections, held in October 2015, and presidential elections held on January 24 were free and fair. Civilian authorities maintained effective control over the security forces.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Portugal is a constitutional democracy with free elections and civilian control of security forces.

propositions.text: Portugal is a functioning democracy able and willing to provide adequate state protection to its citizens, including the Appellant.
propositions.quote: What all of the above tells me, and is unrefuted by any documentary evidence from the Appellant, is that Portugal is a democracy, fully functioning, and is able and willing to provide its citizens adequate state protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to provide evidence to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has failed to adduce any evidence to support his allegation of inadequate state protection and has therefore failed to rebut the presumption.

propositions.text: States are presumed capable of protecting citizens except in complete state breakdown (Ward).
propositions.quote: States are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown. (Ward)

propositions.text: International protection applies only when no other recourse is available (Ward).
propositions.quote: The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. (Ward)

propositions.text: Presumption of state protection applies even if state is alleged persecutor (Hinzman).
propositions.quote: The presumption of state protection applies equally to cases where the state is alleged to be a persecutor. (Hinzman)

propositions.text: Claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence to rebut presumption of state protection (Ward).
propositions.quote: To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens, (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national). (Ward)

propositions.text: Claimant must persuade Board on balance of probabilities that state protection is inadequate (Flores Carrillo).
propositions.quote: A claimant who alleges that the state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo) The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo)

propositions.text: Claimant bears burden to rebut presumption of state protection by clear and convincing evidence (Kaleja).
propositions.quote: Thus RPD is not obliged to prove that the state can offer the claimant effective protection, rather, the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the RPD on a balance of probabilities. (Kaleja)

propositions.text: State's effective control and serious efforts to protect citizens do not require perfect success to maintain presumption (Villafranca).
propositions.quote: Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection. (Villafranca)

propositions.text: Board is not obliged to prove state can offer effective protection (Quintero Sanchez).
propositions.quote: The Board is not obliged to prove that a state can offer its citizens effective state protection. (Quintero Sanchez)

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Portugal provides adequate state protection; the appellant failed to rebut the presumption, citing legal principles on state protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to show any errors of law, fact, or mixed law and fact by the RPD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has failed to convince me that the RPD committed any errors of law, of fact or of mixed law and fact.

propositions.text: The court concurs with the RPD that the Appellant lacks credibility and subjective fear.
propositions.quote: I concur with the RPD that the Appellant lacks credibility and subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error by the RPD and agrees the appellant lacks credibility and subjective fear.

propositions.text: It is reasonable for the RAD to consider state protection even if not fully expounded in the RPD Reasons and Decision.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable for the RAD to consider that issue even if it was not expounded on in the Reasons and Decision, but only mentioned.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not provide evidence before the RPD supporting inadequate state protection in Portugal.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not adduced any evidence before the RPD to support his allegation of inadequate state protection for him, in Portugal.

propositions.text: The court finds state protection in Portugal is at least adequate.
propositions.quote: I find that state protection in Portugal is at least adequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable to consider state protection; the appellant provided no evidence; state protection in Portugal is adequate.

propositions.text: The RAD upholds the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: The RAD has found that the RPD decision will stand.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders that the RPD decision stands.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: This appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA.
